{{Short description|American physicist}}
'''Keith H. Jackson''' was an American physicist, a professor of physics, and former president of the [[National Society of Black Physicists]].

== Life and education ==
Jackson was born in [[Columbus, Ohio]] on September 24, 1953.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |title=Keith Jackson's Biography |url=https://www.thehistorymakers.org/biography/keith-jackson-2 |access-date=2023-10-27 |website=The HistoryMakers |language=en}}</ref> He earned a bachelor's degree in physics from [[Morehouse College]] and a bachelor's degree in electrical engineering at the [[Georgia Tech|Georgia Institute of Technology]].<ref name=":0" />  In 1979, he earned a master's degree from [[Stanford University]] in physics, followed by a Ph.D. in physics in 1982.<ref name=":0" /> His thesis research was in the area of photo-dissociation, and  his advisor was Dr. [[Richard Zare|Richard N. Zare]].<ref name=":2">{{Cite web |last=Williams |first=Scott |title=Physicists of the African Diaspora |url=http://www.math.buffalo.edu/mad/physics/jackson_keith.html |access-date=October 27, 2023 |website=Physicists of the African Diaspora}}</ref> He died of cancer in 2013.<ref name=":3">{{Cite web |last=scyang |date=2017-10-03 |title=How Berkeley Lab Software Helped Lead to the 2017 Nobel Prize in Physics - Berkeley Lab |url=https://newscenter.lbl.gov/2017/10/03/berkeley-lab-tools-helped-ligo-nobel-physics/ |access-date=2023-10-27 |website=Berkeley Lab News Center |language=en-US}}</ref> 

== Career ==
After earning his Ph.D., Jackson worked as part of the Gate Dielectric Group at [[Hewlett-Packard|Hewlett Packard]] Laboratories, and then joined [[Rockwell International]]'s [[Rocketdyne]] division,<ref name=":2" /> where he worked on [[Synthetic diamond|polychrystalline diamond]] thin films.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Thompson |first=Garland |date=January 1, 2004 |title=The 50-Most Important African-Americans in Technology |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=pJ-eJBOwoXUC&dq=howard+university+keith+jackson+physics&pg=PA25 |website=US Black Engineer and IT |page=25}}</ref> In 1992, Jackson became the Associate Director at the [[Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory]]'s (LBNL) Center for X-ray Optics.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |title=IEEE Explore |url=https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/author/37276269600 |access-date=2023-10-27 |website=[[IEEE]]}}</ref> At LBNL, Jackson and his colleagues developed [[Python (programming language)|Python]]-based programming tools that helped physicists efficiently distribute data. One such tool, Py/Globus, was used to efficiently replicate data from the [[Laser Interferometer Gravitational wave Observatory|Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory]] to confirm Albert Einstein’s [[General relativity|General Theory of Relativity]].<ref name=":3" />

His research areas included ultraviolet lithography, [[synchrotron radiation]], fabrication of high aspect ratio microstructures, and imaging studies of [[extreme ultraviolet]] masks.<ref name=":1" /> 

Jackson joined [[Florida A&M University]] as Vice President of Research and Professor of Physics in 2005, and in 2010, he began working at [[Morgan State University]], as the chairperson of the physics department.<ref name=":0" /> 

Jackson was a former president of the [[National Society of Black Physicists]] (NSBP),<ref>{{Cite web |title=NSBP History - National Society of Black Physicists |url=https://nsbp.org/page/NSBPHistory |access-date=2023-10-27 |website=nsbp.org |language=en}}</ref> as well as an NSBP fellow.<ref>{{Cite web |title=NSBP Fellows - National Society of Black Physicists |url=https://nsbp.org/page/NSBPFellows |access-date=2023-10-27 |website=nsbp.org |language=en}}</ref>
